`hostname`: show or set the host's name.

## Synopsis

<strong>hostname</strong>\
<strong>hostname</strong> <em>name</em>\
<strong>hostname -F</strong> <em>file</em>

## Description

With no arguments, <strong>hostname</strong> prints the host's name. Until one is set, it is the first network card's address (in bus order), the address <strong>rsh</strong>(1) finds the computer by anyway; with no network card, <strong>localhost</strong>.

With a <em>name</em>, it sets the name and keeps it in <strong>/etc/hostname</strong>, so the computer has it again after a reboot (the boot's <strong>/etc/rc</strong> reads that file). An empty <em>name</em> unsets it. <strong>rsh</strong> finds a computer by its name, as well as by its card's address.

A name is letters, digits, <strong>-</strong> and <strong>.</strong>, at most 64 of them.

## Options

<strong>-F</strong> <em>file</em>
: Sets the name from the first line of <em>file</em>, keeping nothing.

## Exit status

0 when the name was printed or set; 1 for a name that isn't one, or a file that cannot be read or written.

## Examples

```text
hostname
hostname lab
rsh lab ls
```

## Notes

GNU <strong>hostname</strong>'s <em>name</em> sets it only until the next boot; keeping it is <strong>hostnamectl set-hostname</strong>'s job. mcos's <strong>hostname</strong> does both.

## See also

<strong>rsh</strong>(1), <strong>rshd</strong>(1)
